vulnerabilities.description: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature vulnerability in dashbit nimble_zta allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to authenticate as an arbitrary Cloudflare service token. Applications using the Cloudflare Zero Trust authentication strategy are affected. This issue affects nimble_zta from 0.1.2 before 0.1.3.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. The affected software is not part of Liquibase Secure.

ratings.justification: The affected nimble_zta library is not present in Liquibase Secure.

analysis.detail: False match. The CVE is for nimble_zta, an Elixir authentication library published by dashbit, not for the dash shell. The Ubuntu tracker attributes it to the dash package by name. The Liquibase Secure image ships no Elixir or Erlang runtime and no nimble_zta code.

vulnerabilities.description: A flaw was found in dash. The printf builtin reserves four bytes before converting a Unicode escape (backslash-u or backslash-U), but the multi-byte token can need five or six bytes. A local user who can supply such an escape to dash printf or echo %b, including through dash -c and a positional argument, can write one or two bytes past that reservation.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. The dash version in the image predates the Unicode escape support that carries this flaw.

ratings.justification: dash 0.5.12 has no Unicode escape handling in its printf builtin.

analysis.detail: The overflow is in the printf builtin's handling of the Unicode escapes (backslash-u and backslash-U), which dash gained in 0.5.13 together with dollar-single-quote quoting (upstream commit 776424a8). Ubuntu noble ships dash 0.5.12-6ubuntu5, whose printf.c has no Unicode escape handling and no CHECKSTRSPACE reservation to overrun; the Debian and Ubuntu patch series for 0.5.12 add only the backslash-e escape. The scanner matches on the package name, not on the presence of the code.

vulnerabilities.description: A flaw was found in dash. When built without libc fnmatch, the internal pmatch() matcher implements * by unbounded recursion over candidate positions. A local user who can plant filenames, or otherwise feed that matcher, can make a short multi-star pattern such as *.*.*.*.*.tar.gz consume excessive CPU.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: No action required. No shipped code path invokes dash; Liquibase and its entrypoint use bash or exec binaries directly.

ratings.justification: No untrusted input reaches dash; nothing in the image invokes /bin/sh.

analysis.detail: Ubuntu builds dash with --disable-fnmatch, so the recursive pmatch matcher is present in 0.5.12-6ubuntu5. Reaching it needs dash to evaluate a multi-star pattern (globbing, case, ${var#pat}) against attacker-influenced names. Nothing in the image runs dash: /bin/sh is dash, but the entrypoint and the liquibase launcher are bash scripts, Liquibase's flow shell action runs bash -c, and its executeCommand change and other ProcessBuilder call sites exec the named binary directly without a shell. lpm is a static Go binary that spawns no processes on Linux. Only the operator who authors the changelog or flow file can invoke dash explicitly, and that operator already controls the container; the impact would be CPU exhaustion of their own unprivileged process.
